interview_metadata.name: Saba Guevara
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) ??? Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in Yuba City, so my whole life has kind of been in this mix of orchards, strip malls, family parties, and a lot of different cultures living close together. My dad's side came from Uzbekistan in the early 2000s, and my mom's family is Mexican, so at home I grew up hearing English, Uzbek, Spanish, and sometimes Russian when my dad was talking to older relatives. My childhood was pretty normal but busy. School, helping my mom, family gatherings, Navruz in the spring, Dia de los Muertos with my mom's relatives, and a lot of food around all of it. I was a decent student, not the top person in class, but I liked art projects, photography, and anything where I could make something look organized or pretty. After high school I did not go straight to college because money was tight and I was tired of school, so I started working retail. At first it was just a job, but I realized I was good at helping customers, setting up displays, and noticing what people actually buy. I am 23 now, never married, no kids, still living in Yuba City with my family, and trying to build from where I am. I want to become a department lead, then eventually a store manager, and later open a small boutique that mixes Central Asian patterns with modern clothing. My life has not had one dramatic movie moment, but it has had a lot of small choices about whether to stay comfortable or push myself.

follow_ups.question: When you think about childhood at home, what routines or traditions stand out most?
follow_ups.response: Food is the biggest one. On weekends my dad would make plov in a big pot, and my mom would make rice, beans, or tamales if her sisters were coming over. Around Navruz we would clean the house and have relatives over, and around Dia de los Muertos my mom put out photos and marigolds.

follow_ups.question: Who were you closest to growing up?
follow_ups.response: Probably my mom day to day, because she was easier to talk to, but my dad shaped my work ethic. I was also close with my younger brother Timur because I helped watch him after school when my parents worked.

follow_ups.question: What did you imagine your adult life would look like when you were in high school?
follow_ups.response: I thought I might do something creative, maybe fashion or photography, but I did not have a clean plan. I mostly knew I wanted to earn my own money and not feel stuck.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was after high school in 2020. I had friends going to community college right away, some leaving Yuba City, and I felt like if I stayed home and worked people would think I had no ambition. At the same time, my family needed help with bills and I was not sure what I wanted to study. I took a retail job thinking it would be temporary, and at first I felt embarrassed when classmates came in. Then my manager asked me to redo a sale display because I kept fixing it anyway, and that display actually moved a lot of clearance items. That was the first time I thought, okay, maybe I can turn this into something. I chose to stay working, save money, learn the store, and plan to take business classes later instead of rushing into college just to say I was enrolled.

follow_ups.question: What options did you feel you had at that moment?
follow_ups.response: Community college, moving to Sacramento with a friend, or staying home and working. Moving sounded fun but expensive, and college felt vague because I did not know my major.

follow_ups.question: Who influenced that decision the most?
follow_ups.response: My parents, but not in a controlling way. My mom told me not to take on classes if I was not serious yet, and my dad kept saying any work can teach you if you pay attention.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel about that choice now?
follow_ups.response: Mixed but mostly okay. I wish I had started one or two business classes earlier, but I do not regret learning real work habits first.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was partly conscious and partly just life moving. I consciously decided not to enroll in classes that first semester, but the retail path happened because I needed a paycheck and then discovered I was good at parts of it.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk it through with anyone before deciding?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly with my mom and one friend, Marisol. My dad gave advice too, but he is more like, do the practical thing and stop overthinking.

follow_ups.question: Was there a point when it stopped feeling temporary?
follow_ups.response: Yes, probably after about a year, when I started training newer cashiers and my manager trusted me with inventory counts.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. I think if high school had better career counseling for people who were not going straight to a four-year college, I would have felt less lost. A clear path for retail management, business certificates, or apprenticeships would have helped.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have made the biggest difference?
follow_ups.response: Someone sitting down with me and mapping costs, timelines, and local programs. I needed practical steps, not just posters saying apply to college.

follow_ups.question: Did your workplace provide any guidance like that?
follow_ups.response: A little. My current manager talks to me about becoming a lead, but formal training is still pretty thin.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am not married, I do not have kids, and I am not living with a romantic partner. My family is still the center of my life, even when they get on my nerves. My mom, Rosa, is the person I talk to most, especially when I am stressed about money or work. My dad, Dilshod, is quieter but very present; he is the one who will fix something, drive someone to an appointment, or remind me to save money. My younger brother Timur is 16, and I help him with rides sometimes or make sure he eats something besides chips. I also have a lot of extended family around Northern California. My mom's side gathers for birthdays and holidays, and my dad's Uzbek friends feel like aunties and uncles even if they are not blood relatives. I dated someone last year for a few months, but right now I am single and focused on work.

follow_ups.question: How often do you spend time with your parents outside basic household routines?
follow_ups.response: A few times a week. Sometimes it is just tea after dinner, grocery runs, or cooking together on Sunday.

follow_ups.question: What is your relationship with your brother like day to day?
follow_ups.response: It is half sibling annoyance and half protective. I tease him about gaming too much, but I also take him to volleyball or pick him up if my parents are working.

follow_ups.question: Are you dating anyone now?
follow_ups.response: No, not seriously. I will go out if someone asks and it feels easy, but I am not trying to build my schedule around dating right now.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have an older half-sister on my mom's side, Elena, who lives in Sacramento. We are friendly and text, but she has her own life and a little kid, so we mostly see each other at family events.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Elena?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once every month or two, more during holidays.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel close to her child?
follow_ups.response: Yes, my niece is little and funny. I am not babysitting every week, but I like bringing her small gifts.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friends are Marisol and Anya. Marisol and I went to high school together, and she is the person I text when something ridiculous happens at work. Anya is from a language-exchange meetup, and we practice Russian and Uzbek phrases and talk about books. I also have coworkers I like, especially Janelle, who works fitting rooms and has good style. We sometimes get coffee after closing. My social life is not huge, but it is steady: food, walks, festivals, volleyball meetups, and sending each other memes.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your friends in person?
follow_ups.response: Usually once or twice a week if schedules line up. Retail schedules make it annoying, so sometimes it is just a late coffee or a walk.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Marisol usually do together?
follow_ups.response: We get tacos, go to Target even when we do not need anything, or drive around taking photos if the light is good.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Yuba City in a pretty ordinary neighborhood, mostly small houses, families, older people, and some rentals. It is not fancy, but it is familiar. We are close enough to grocery stores, taquerias, and my work that I do not feel cut off, but you still need a car for most things. I like that Yuba City has different communities layered together: Punjabi families, Mexican families, people from Central Asia, long-time local families. You notice it in food stores, festivals, and languages you hear. The downside is there is not a ton to do if you want nightlife or bigger art events, so I go to Sacramento sometimes.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually go nearby for errands?
follow_ups.response: WinCo or Grocery Outlet for basics, a Mexican market for tortillas and produce, and sometimes an Asian or international market when we need rice, spices, or noodles.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A few. We wave, and my mom knows more people than I do. One older neighbor gives us lemons sometimes.

follow_ups.question: What places in Yuba City feel most like yours?
follow_ups.response: The river paths, local festivals, the grocery stores where everyone is buying giant bags of rice, and little coffee spots where I can sit with my camera.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe, especially during the day. At night I pay attention, lock my car, and do not walk alone in certain parking lots, but I am not scared living here.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened that shaped that feeling?
follow_ups.response: Mostly car break-ins around town and hearing about stuff on Facebook groups. Nothing major has happened to me personally.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents feel the same way?
follow_ups.response: My mom is more cautious and always tells me to text when I get home. My dad acts relaxed but checks the doors twice.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is family, affordability compared to bigger cities, and feeling known. The downside is fewer career options, fewer creative spaces, and sometimes feeling like people expect you to stay in the same lane forever.

follow_ups.question: Do you see yourself staying in Yuba City?
follow_ups.response: For now, yes. Long term I could see Sacramento or maybe somewhere with more fashion retail, but I would still want family close.

follow_ups.question: What would make the area better for you?
follow_ups.response: More local arts events, better public transit, and more jobs where young people can grow without leaving.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me, my mom Rosa, my dad Dilshod, and my younger brother Timur. My parents rent the house, and I contribute every month. We all have our routines, but the kitchen is the main shared space. My dad leaves early for warehouse work, my mom has a medical office schedule, I have changing retail shifts, and Timur is in high school. Nobody else is staying with us right now.

follow_ups.question: How do household chores get divided?
follow_ups.response: My mom does the most organizing, honestly. I cook one or two nights, clean the kitchen, and help with grocery shopping. Timur gets trash and yard stuff when he remembers.

follow_ups.question: Do you have your own room?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I have my own room, small but mine. It is where I keep my clothes, camera, and too many half-finished decor projects.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent right now.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone stayed temporarily in the past year?
follow_ups.response: My aunt stayed for a week after a surgery, but not long-term.

follow_ups.question: Would your family take someone in if needed?
follow_ups.response: Probably, yes. My parents are very hospitality-first, even when the house feels crowded.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes cousins sleep over after family gatherings, but nobody regularly stays here.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a few times a year.

follow_ups.question: Where do they sleep when they visit?
follow_ups.response: Usually the couch or an air mattress in the living room.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everyone who usually lives here is currently here.

follow_ups.question: No one away at college or military service?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any hospital or care facility stays right now?
follow_ups.response: No, thankfully.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My week depends on the retail schedule. If I open, I wake up around 6:30, make coffee, maybe toast or yogurt, and get to work before 8. If I close, I sleep later, do errands or take a walk with my camera, then work afternoon to evening. Weekends are usually busier at the store, so I do not always have Saturday off. On a good week I fit in one trail run by the river, one volleyball meetup, and one dinner with friends or family. Sundays, if I am not working, are cooking and laundry days.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 11:30 on normal nights, later if I close and come home wired.

follow_ups.question: Which day feels most predictable?
follow_ups.response: Usually Monday or Tuesday because the store is slower, but my days off change.

follow_ups.question: What is a typical errand day like?
follow_ups.response: Groceries, gas, maybe returns, maybe taking my brother somewhere, and then I try to squeeze in an iced coffee or photos.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work retail sales at an apparel and home goods store in the Yuba City area. I am on the floor helping customers, running register, restocking, checking inventory, and setting up displays. My schedule is usually 32 to 36 hours a week, sometimes closer to 40 during holidays or big sales. Shifts can be 8 to 4, 11 to 7, or 1 to 9:30 if I close. I like the customer side more than I expected, especially when I can help someone build an outfit or find a gift.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job are you best at?
follow_ups.response: Visual merchandising and reading customers. I can usually tell if someone wants help or wants space.

follow_ups.question: What part is most draining?
follow_ups.response: Messy clearance racks and customers who treat staff like we are invisible.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help at home more than it probably sounds. I help with groceries, translation sometimes when older Uzbek relatives need forms or appointment help, and I drive my brother if my parents are stuck at work. I also try to meal prep rice, chicken, or soup so I do not spend all my money eating out. I am not perfectly organized, but I keep lists in my notes app. I also spend time looking at retail management videos or small business content because I want to move up.

follow_ups.question: What languages do you translate between?
follow_ups.response: Mostly Uzbek to English, sometimes simple Russian, and Spanish with my mom's relatives if needed.

follow_ups.question: What do you meal prep most often?
follow_ups.response: Rice bowls, lentil soup, chicken with cumin and coriander, or leftovers from plov if we made a big pot.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Recently I have been taking more closing shifts because one coworker left, so my evenings are less free. I also started doing short morning runs because if I wait until after work, I usually skip it. Another change is that I am looking at community college business classes again for the fall. That means I am trying to be less random with spending and sleep, though I am still not great at it.

follow_ups.question: How many mornings a week are you running?
follow_ups.response: Two if I am realistic, three if the schedule is kind.

follow_ups.question: What class are you considering first?
follow_ups.response: Probably intro business or marketing, something that connects to retail and eventually my boutique idea.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so that does not apply to me. The closest thing is helping with my brother's schedule sometimes, like rides after school or reminding him about assignments.

follow_ups.question: Do you expect to have children someday?
follow_ups.response: Maybe someday, but not soon. I want more stability and my own place first.

follow_ups.question: What after-school things does your brother do?
follow_ups.response: He plays casual volleyball and mostly hangs out with friends or games online.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My personal experiences have been limited. I have been pulled over once for a brake light and got a warning. At work we call security more than police, usually for shoplifting or someone yelling. I do notice that my dad gets nervous around police even though he has not done anything, probably from being an immigrant and not wanting any trouble. I am respectful, but I do not see police as automatically safe for everyone.

follow_ups.question: What happened during the brake light stop?
follow_ups.response: It was quick. I was nervous, gave my license, and the officer told me to fix it. My dad replaced the bulb that weekend.

follow_ups.question: Have police ever come to your home?
follow_ups.response: No, not for us.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Mostly watching things happen around stores. There was one time a man was clearly having some kind of mental health or drug issue near the entrance, and I remember wishing someone trained for crisis response came instead of just police.

follow_ups.question: Did that incident affect customers or staff?
follow_ups.response: Yes, people were nervous and staff did not know what to do besides call security.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone get hurt?
follow_ups.response: No, but it felt tense.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I have a cousin on my mom's side who had a DUI a few years ago, but we are not super close. In my immediate family, no arrests.

follow_ups.question: Did your cousin's DUI affect the family?
follow_ups.response: It was talked about for a while, mostly as a warning. My mom used it to lecture all of us about rides and planning.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about legal issues for anyone close to you?
follow_ups.response: Not really.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote, but I am not perfect about every local thing. I voted in 2020 and 2024, and I try to vote in California elections because things like wages, rent, and health care actually affect us. Local races are harder because I do not always know who people are, so I read the voter guide and sometimes ask friends. I vote by mail because it is easier with my schedule.

follow_ups.question: Who first encouraged you to vote?
follow_ups.response: My high school government teacher and my mom. My mom is very serious about voting because her parents did not always feel heard.

follow_ups.question: Do your friends vote?
follow_ups.response: Some do, some forget. I usually remind Marisol when ballots come.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would say I am left-leaning but practical. I care about workers being paid enough, health care being affordable, immigration being treated with basic respect, and people not being judged for their background. At the same time, I get skeptical when politicians talk like they understand working families but never make anything simpler. I am not super ideological; I look at whether a policy would help people I know. Minimum wage, rent costs, community college, and small business support matter to me. I am also pro-choice and supportive of LGBTQ people. On crime, I want safety, but I do not think more punishment fixes everything. I guess I am a Democrat most of the time, but not someone who thinks the party is perfect.

follow_ups.question: What issues feel most personal to you?
follow_ups.response: Wages, health care, immigration, and education costs. Those are the things I see in my own household and at work.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with your parents?
follow_ups.response: A little. My mom is more Democratic, my dad is practical and sometimes suspicious of all politicians.

follow_ups.question: What makes you skeptical of politicians?
follow_ups.response: They promise help but forms, costs, and rules stay confusing. Working people do not have time to decode everything.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more interested in local politics than before. When I was younger, national politics felt like the only thing people argued about. Now I care more about city decisions, rent, roads, public safety, and whether there are programs for young adults to get training. I have also become more skeptical of social media politics because everything gets flattened into a fight. I still lean Democratic, but I try not to repost something just because it sounds right.

follow_ups.question: What made local politics feel more important?
follow_ups.response: Paying bills and driving around town. You realize potholes, transit, housing, and local jobs are not abstract.

follow_ups.question: Have your views shifted on any specific issue?
follow_ups.response: I think I have gotten more realistic about small business costs. I still support worker protections, but I also see how hard it is to run a shop.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It affected me somewhat to a lot. I am not Black, so I do not want to act like it is my exact experience, but being mixed, Latina, and from an immigrant family makes me aware of how people get treated differently. In 2020 I watched videos and read stories that were upsetting. It made me think about policing, but also about race in stores, schools, and everyday assumptions. At work, I notice which customers get watched more closely, and that bothers me.

follow_ups.question: Did you discuss it at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially with my mom. My dad listened but did not always say much.

follow_ups.question: Did it change anything you do at work?
follow_ups.response: It made me more conscious about not profiling customers and speaking up gently if coworkers make assumptions.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the main thing is accountability and whether some communities are treated like threats before anyone knows them. I also think people get stuck on slogans instead of listening to what is underneath: fear, grief, and wanting equal treatment. I do not have a perfect policy answer, but I support better training, body cameras, crisis response teams, and consequences when officers abuse power. I also think schools and jobs have to look at bias, not just police.

follow_ups.question: What do you mean by people getting stuck on slogans?
follow_ups.response: People argue over the phrase and stop hearing the actual stories. That happens a lot on Facebook.

follow_ups.question: Do you think reform is possible?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but only if departments and cities actually collect data and listen to the people most affected.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race is always there, even when people say they do not see it. In my own life, people read me different ways depending on my name, how I look, or what language I am speaking. Sometimes I am Latina, sometimes people ask if I am Middle Eastern, sometimes they just say exotic, which I hate. I think the U.S. talks about diversity like it is food and festivals, but not always about power, money, housing, and who gets believed.

follow_ups.question: Can you remember a recent moment when your background affected how someone treated you?
follow_ups.response: A customer asked if I was allowed to work here because I was speaking Uzbek on the phone with my aunt. It was not violent, just rude and weird.

follow_ups.question: How did you respond?
follow_ups.response: I kept it professional and said yes, I work here, how can I help you. Then I complained to Janelle later.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I talked with family and friends, posted a few resources in 2020, and donated a small amount once, but I did not go to big protests. I am more of a conversation and daily behavior person than a front-line protest person.

follow_ups.question: Why did you not join protests?
follow_ups.response: Partly COVID, partly my parents worrying, and partly I was not sure where I fit.

follow_ups.question: What daily behavior matters to you?
follow_ups.response: How I treat customers, what jokes I ignore or do not ignore, and whether I listen when someone describes something I have not lived.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My friends mostly care, but they respond differently. Marisol posts more and gets into arguments online. Anya reads more and talks quietly. My mom gets emotional because she remembers being treated like she was less educated just because of her accent or Spanish. My dad is more cautious; he agrees people get treated unfairly, but he worries protests can become chaotic or misunderstood.

follow_ups.question: Have these differences caused conflict?
follow_ups.response: Not major conflict, but some tense conversations at family gatherings.

follow_ups.question: Who do you learn from most on this topic?
follow_ups.response: Friends who share personal stories, not influencers. Real examples make me think more.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I am pretty healthy. I do not have a chronic diagnosis, and I can work on my feet all day, which I do not take for granted. My main issues are stress, sleep getting messy with closing shifts, and sometimes back or foot pain after long retail days. I try to run or walk the river paths and play casual volleyball, but I am not a strict fitness person. I could eat more consistently and drink more water.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise in a normal week?
follow_ups.response: Two or three times if walks count. Real running maybe twice.

follow_ups.question: What do you do for foot or back pain?
follow_ups.response: Better shoes, stretching, hot showers, and sometimes ibuprofen.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy when I have a morning shift and can cook dinner at home. It is hard when I close, come home tired, and want fast food or snacks. Money matters too, because healthy food is not always expensive if you cook, but time and planning are the problem. My family cooks real food, which helps, but we also make heavy rice dishes.

follow_ups.question: What healthy foods do you actually like?
follow_ups.response: Soups, grilled chicken, cucumbers and tomatoes, yogurt, fruit, and lentils.

follow_ups.question: What throws you off fastest?
follow_ups.response: Closing shifts and stress. I snack too much when I get home late.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge. I twisted my ankle during a trail run last year and had to take it easy for a few weeks. I also had a period of bad sleep and headaches when work was understaffed during the holidays. No major diagnosis, no broken bones. I did get a regular checkup because my mom kept pushing me, and everything was basically fine.

follow_ups.question: Did you get medical care for the ankle?
follow_ups.response: I went to urgent care because it swelled up, but it was just a sprain.

follow_ups.question: What helped the headaches?
follow_ups.response: Sleep, less caffeine late, and trying to eat before shifts.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not stopped me from working, except missing one shift for the ankle. The bigger issue is fatigue making me less patient or less motivated after work.

follow_ups.question: Do you have paid sick time?
follow_ups.response: Some sick time, yes, but I try not to use it unless I really need to.

follow_ups.question: Why avoid using it?
follow_ups.response: Partly guilt and partly knowing the floor gets short-staffed.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, more with family than me. My dad has high blood pressure and my mom worries about blood sugar because it runs in her family. My aunt had surgery last year, and she stayed with us briefly while she recovered. It was not a crisis, but it changed the house rhythm. In immigrant families, health stuff becomes everyone's business because someone has to translate, drive, cook, or remind people to take medicine.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with your dad's blood pressure care?
follow_ups.response: Mostly reminders about appointments and trying not to cook everything too salty.

follow_ups.question: Who usually handles family medical paperwork?
follow_ups.response: My mom, but I help when there are forms or online portals.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: Getting appointments can be annoying, but we manage. I have delayed dental care because it felt expensive and not urgent. We do not avoid emergency care, but we definitely ask, how much is this going to cost?

follow_ups.question: When did you delay dental care?

follow_ups.question: How do you choose where to go for care?

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Yes, informal stuff, but not instead of doctors for serious things. My dad drinks herbal teas, and my mom uses vapor rub, teas, and home remedies from her mom. I am open to it if it is harmless, but I am skeptical of anything that tells you to skip real medical care.

follow_ups.question: What remedy do you actually use?
follow_ups.response: Honey lemon tea and soup. I also do steam when congested.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever disagreed with family about remedies?

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink socially, usually one or two drinks if I am out with friends or at a family event, but not as my main coping thing. If I am stressed, I am more likely to snack, scroll, play a game, or take a walk. I have seen alcohol cause drama in extended family, so I am careful with it.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually drink socially?
follow_ups.response: A margarita, cider, or wine if we are in wine country.

follow_ups.question: How often would you say you drink?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a couple times a month, not weekly most months.

transcript.response: I do not use prescriptions for coping, and I do not really use marijuana. I tried an edible once with friends and did not like feeling out of control, so I have not repeated it. For pain I use over-the-counter ibuprofen or acetaminophen when needed. Most recent was ibuprofen after a long closing shift when my feet and lower back hurt.

follow_ups.question: When was the edible experience?
follow_ups.response: About two years ago at a friend's apartment.

follow_ups.question: Do people around you use marijuana?

transcript.response: We mostly use insurance through my parents' jobs and I have coverage through my workplace option, though the plan is not amazing. For me, the main thing is not letting small stuff turn into expensive stuff, but sometimes I still procrastinate.

follow_ups.question: Do you understand your own insurance plan?

follow_ups.question: Do medical costs cause household stress?

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?

follow_ups.question: Was your family on the same page?
follow_ups.response: Mostly yes. Some extended relatives were skeptical, but my immediate family got vaccinated.

follow_ups.question: Do you get flu shots?
follow_ups.response: Not every year, but I have gotten them, especially when work is crowded.

transcript.response: I trust doctors, public health websites, and pharmacists more than random posts. My mom works around medical office people, so she asks questions there. follow_ups.question: Do you discuss medical information in family chats?
follow_ups.response: Yes, and sometimes it gets messy because relatives forward things without checking.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: This past year has been up and down. I am not miserable, but I have had stretches where I felt restless, like I should be further ahead by now. Seeing people online move out, get degrees, or travel makes me compare myself even when I know that is not fair. Work can be tiring, but it also gives me structure and confidence. I feel best when I am making concrete progress, like saving money, improving a display, or planning a class. I feel worst when I am scrolling late at night and thinking I am behind.

follow_ups.response: My mom notices fast. Marisol also notices because I stop replying normally.

It was not a huge disaster, but I went home and cried because I felt stupid and replaceable. My mom made tea and basically told me to sleep before deciding my life was over. The next day I apologized to my manager, fixed the count, and realized I was exhausted more than incapable.

follow_ups.response: Navruz gatherings, remembering relatives, lighting candles with my mom, and family meals where older people tell stories.
